title: TRAINING LLM-BASED TUTORS TO IMPROVE STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES IN DIALOGUES
venue: AIED 2025: The 26th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to improve LLM-based tutoring systems so that they do not merely sound pedagogically appropriate, but are trained to generate tutor responses that are more likely to improve student performance during tutoring dialogues. The authors argue that prior LLM tutors are usually optimized to follow tutoring principles or prompts, but not explicitly optimized for student learning outcomes across turns of dialogue. Their core research question is whether an open-source LLM tutor can be trained to produce utterances that both preserve pedagogical quality and increase the likelihood that a student responds correctly on the next turn.

The intervention is a training pipeline for an AI math tutor based on Llama 3.1 8B. The approach first generates multiple candidate tutor utterances from several sources, including human tutors, GPT-4o, and smaller Llama models. Each candidate is then scored on two dimensions: predicted student correctness using LLMKT, a dialogue knowledge-tracing student model, and pedagogical quality using a hand-crafted rubric judged by GPT-4o. These scores are combined to construct preference pairs, and the tutor model is fine-tuned using direct preference optimization (DPO), after an initial distillation stage from GPT-4o outputs. The paper also includes automated evaluation, qualitative analysis, and a small-scale human evaluation.

The context is one-on-one math tutoring dialogues from the MathDial dataset, which is grounded in GSM8K math word problems. In this dataset, tutors are crowd workers and students are simulated by GPT-3.5 rather than real learners, so the study takes place in a simulated dialogue environment rather than an authentic classroom deployment. The paper concerns K-12 math tutoring in general, but no exact grade band is reported. Human evaluation was conducted with two volunteer university students as annotators, but they were evaluators rather than the learner population under study.

The main conclusion is that the DPO-trained open-source tutor substantially improves predicted next-turn student correctness compared with the baselines, including GPT-4o, while maintaining pedagogical quality comparable to GPT-4o. Qualitative results suggest the model learns to ask more manageable, scaffolded questions that help students make progress without directly giving away answers. However, the authors explicitly note that the most important limitation is the absence of real students in the experiments; outcomes are based on simulated student modeling and rubric judgments rather than actual learning gains. They position the work as a promising starting point that requires future validation in real educational settings with real students and longer-term learning outcomes.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta's LLaMA family of large language models, used here as the base family for an open-source dialogue tutor model fine-tuned for math tutoring.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper fine-tunes LLaMA (specifically Llama 3.1 8B) via distillation from GPT-4o-generated tutor utterances and then direct preference optimization to generate math tutor dialogue turns that maximize predicted next-turn student correctness while maintaining pedagogical quality.

findings.finding_summary: On the MathDial test set, the DPO-trained LLaMA tutor achieved a student outcome score of 0.65 on LLMKT-predicted next-turn correctness, compared with 0.47 for the distilled LLaMA model, 0.43 for the base LLaMA model, and 0.49 for GPT-4o. The authors state this is a 33% improvement over the next best method (GPT-4o), indicating the optimized LLaMA tutor was most likely to elicit correct student responses under the student model.
findings.measure: Average LLMKT-predicted probability of correct student response on the next tutor-student turn
findings.effect_size: 0.65 vs 0.49 GPT-4o; 33% improvement over next best method

findings.finding_summary: The DPO-trained LLaMA tutor scored 9.37 overall on the GPT-4o pedagogical rubric, closely matching GPT-4o's 9.40 and outperforming the distilled LLaMA model's 8.93. On rubric components, DPO reached Acc.=0.97, Prog.=0.96, Err.=0.92, Hint.=0.96, Wth.=0.99, and Enc.=0.92, showing strong pedagogical quality alongside improved predicted student correctness.
findings.measure: GPT-4o rubric-based pedagogical evaluation of tutor utterances (overall 1-10 score and rubric item scores)

findings.finding_summary: In human evaluation, the DPO-trained LLaMA tutor was ranked best for likely leading to a correct student response (average correctness rank 1.75, where rank 1 is best), compared with 2.12 for human tutors and 2.13 for GPT-4o. It also received the highest human rubric score, 8.55 versus 8.07 for GPT-4o and 7.36 for human tutors; all differences were reported as statistically significant at p < 0.05 by paired t-test.
findings.measure: Human-ranked likelihood of eliciting correct student response and human pedagogical rubric score

findings.finding_summary: When varying the preference-weight parameter λ from 0.00 to 1.00 on a 500-turn-pair subset, increasing λ generally increased predicted student correctness while generally decreasing pedagogical rubric score. The paper reports that values around 0.5 to 0.75 maintained relatively high pedagogical scores while substantially improving predicted correctness, suggesting a tradeoff rather than a uniformly dominant setting.
findings.measure: Tradeoff between LLMKT-predicted correctness and pedagogical rubric score as λ varies

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT family of large language models, used here both as a tutor utterance generator and as an automated evaluator of pedagogical quality.
identified_tools.use_case: GPT-4o was used to generate candidate tutor utterances for math dialogues and to judge tutor utterances with a pedagogical rubric; GPT-3.5 appears only as the simulated student source in the underlying MathDial dataset, not as the focal intervention.

findings.finding_summary: As a tutor-generation baseline, ChatGPT (GPT-4o) achieved a student outcome score of 0.49 on LLMKT-predicted next-turn correctness and an overall pedagogical rubric score of 9.40 on the MathDial test set. This made it second-best on predicted correctness behind the DPO-trained LLaMA model, while remaining the top automated rubric scorer by a small margin.
findings.measure: Average LLMKT-predicted probability of correct student response and GPT-4o rubric-based pedagogical score

findings.finding_summary: In human evaluation, ChatGPT (GPT-4o) had an average correctness rank of 2.13 and a rubric score of 8.07, both below the DPO-trained LLaMA tutor (1.75 and 8.55, respectively). The paper reports these differences were statistically significant at p < 0.05, suggesting that although GPT-4o performed strongly, it was not the best-performing tutor in human judgment.
findings.measure: Human-ranked likelihood of eliciting correct student response and human pedagogical rubric score

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical study with quantitative automated evaluation and a small human evaluation, but it does not test the tutor with real students; the main outcome is simulated student correctness predicted by LLMKT on an existing dialogue dataset. Because the evidence is based on offline modeling rather than RCT/QED with authentic learners, the study fits yellow-tier evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are large on the paper's primary metric: the DPO-trained LLaMA tutor improves predicted student correctness from 0.49 to 0.65 versus the next best method, which the authors describe as a 33% improvement. However, this strong impact is on simulated/offline outcomes rather than real-world student achievement.
